summary: Speaking to devotees at a festival in Russia, Indradyumna Swami makes the case for reviving Harinam Sankirtan—congregational chanting of the holy name in public—as the original 'trademark' of Lord Chaitanya's movement. He explains that Lord Chaitanya, the yuga-avatara who gives the yuga-dharma of chanting Hare Krishna in the age of Kali, took the holy name out of the private, locked house of Srivas Thakur and onto the streets of Nadia, a 'spiritual revolution' that let common people—not only the intellectual one percent—make real advancement, though it drew ridicule (Mayavadi sannyasis at Kashi dismissed him as a madman) and even persecution (Haridas Thakur was jailed for street chanting). He traces how Srila Prabhupada brought Sankirtan to the West from humble beginnings—illustrated by the 'do-not shop' story and the first self-conscious chanting party at 26 Second Avenue—and how book distribution, the 'Brihat Mridanga' that can be heard all over the world, later grew into the main preaching activity, unfortunately at Harinam's expense. Citing Tamala Krishna Goswami's counsel to 'find the balance' ('why this or that—why not both?'), he insists the two angas need not compete but can go on side by side, especially now that a country like Russia has thousands of devotees. Much of the talk is practical: because devotees are effectively competing with modern advertising, Harinam must be done first-class—dress in one's best, decorate the mridangas and shine the kartals, sing melodies one can actually perform well, print attractive invitations, dance in choreographed patterns, and never turn one's back on the public, since 'attention to detail is a sign of love.' The aim is to attract every sense: the eyes by ecstatic display, the ears by the sweet holy name, the tongue by prasadam, and the mind and intelligence by invitations, books, and announcements of upcoming programs. Finally he stresses that the external form is only half—the essence is the internal mood of compassion, the wish to share one's good fortune and relieve suffering souls, which makes Sankirtan 'the highest welfare work' and a 'magic formula' that, even when there is no immediate response, plants a seed sure to fructify.
key_points: Lord Chaitanya as the yuga-avatara established the yuga-dharma of congregational chanting: before him devotees chanted privately with their bead bags, but he took the holy name out of Srivas Thakur's locked house onto the streets of Nadia—mass Harinam Sankirtan.

Harinam reaches the common masses whom philosophy and renunciation cannot ('power to the people')—man, woman, child, anyone can make tangible advancement, not just the intellectual one percent who go to the forest or ashram.

Srila Prabhupada revived Sankirtan in the West from humble beginnings; book distribution—the 'Brihat Mridanga' heard all over the world—became the main anga, but it should not eclipse Harinam. Do both and 'find the balance' (Tamala Krishna Goswami).

Difference between the two angas: book distribution is often indirect, done in karmi (non-devotional) clothes with Prabhupada's permission, sometimes not even naming Krishna; Harinam presents Krishna consciousness 'as it is,' a glimpse of Goloka Vrindavan where all walking is dancing, all talking is singing, and there is a festival every day.

Practical standards for first-class Harinam, since it competes with modern advertising (billboards, TV, internet): best dress and gopi-dots (a tradition begun on the Polish festival tour), decorated instruments, matching socks, singable melodies (don't imitate complex tunes and produce a 'perverted reflection'), colorful invitations, choreographed dancing, and never turning your back on the people—Sankirtan is about communication.

Attract all the senses: eyes by the display of spiritual ecstasy, ears by the sweet holy name, tongue by prasadam, and mind/intelligence by invitations, accompanying book distribution, short philosophy talks, and advertising an upcoming event; Sri Prahlad's unpublished Harinam manual, based on Prabhupada's quotes, is recommended for the details.

The internal mood is the real essence—without it the formula won't work. The devotee goes out from compassion, to share his good fortune and relieve souls suffering even in the wealthiest countries; tolerating heat, cold and the restless mind, this makes Harinam the 'highest welfare work' and a transcendental 'magic formula' that plants a seed sure to fructify.
references: Brihan-naradiya Purana — 'harer nama harer nama harer nama eva kevalam / kalau nasty eva nasty eva nasty eva gatir anyatha': in Kali-yuga there is no other way, no other way, no other way to self-realization than chanting the holy name (the same verse is quoted in Chaitanya-charitamrita Adi 17.21).

Bhagavad-gita 2.59 — 'param drstva nivartate': one gives up the lower taste by experiencing a higher taste; cited to explain how Harinam very easily gives the 'higher taste' that keeps devotees fixed in Krishna consciousness.

Nectar of Instruction (Upadeshamrita) verse 1, Rupa Goswami — 'vaco vegam manasah krodha-vegam / jihva-vegam udaropastha-vegam': controlling the urges of speech, mind, anger, tongue, belly and genitals; cited for Sankirtan being 'all about sense control.'

Siksastakam verse 1, Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu — 'anandambudhi-vardhanam': the holy name expands the ever-increasing ocean of transcendental bliss; cited for the pleasure of Harinam always increasing, never deteriorating.

Traditional Sanskrit invocation 'mukam karoti vacalam pangum langhayate girim' — paraphrased by the speaker as: by the mercy of Lord Chaitanya even a blind man can see the stars, a deaf-and-dumb person can recite elegant poetry, and a lame person can climb mountains (verse number not specified to avoid guessing).
Rupa Goswami — describes Sankirtan (of which Harinam is an integral part) as the 'highest welfare work' (para-upakara); speaker does not give a verse number.

Bhaktivinoda Thakura — quoted prayer: 'When will my compassion for all fallen souls manifest, and with a lowly heart in a mood of humility I will go out to preach the divine command' (source song not named by speaker). Also cited: 'man's glory lies in his common sense.'

Non-scriptural sayings cited: Srila Prabhupada — 'the most important instruction is the last one,' 'if you want to please me, distribute my books,' and 'attention to detail is a sign of love'; Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Thakura — 'if you ever get money, print books' (spoken at Radha-kunda) and, in closing, 'this preaching will do good for you and it will do good for others.'
stories: The 'do-not' shop — passing a donut shop where his students took coffee and cigarettes, Prabhupada renamed it the 'do-not' shop: do not be my student and go there.
The first chanting party — the self-conscious early devotees at 26 Second Avenue with a big bass drum and dhotis pinned like diapers, captured on an old video.
Coming down from LSD — hippies would take acid at night and drop into the Bowery morning program to hear Swamiji and get something good to eat.
Haridas Thakura jailed — persecuted and imprisoned for the 'crime' of singing Hare Krishna in the streets.
Kashi sannyasis call him mad — strict Mayavadi renunciants at Benares wrote off the singing, dancing Chaitanya as a madman, not knowing He was the Supreme Lord.
Why not both? — asked to choose between two services, Tamala Krishna Goswami answered 'why this or that? Why not both?' — find the balance.
A flock of canaries — in the early days every devotee, men and women, wore light yellow, so the party looked like a flock of canary birds.
Broken drum vs. billboards — a shabby party with mismatched socks and an unpolished drum cannot compete with the advertising of billboards, TV, and the internet.
quotes: This is like a spiritual revolution.
attention to detail is a sign of love

glossary.meaning: Congregational chanting of the holy names in public, the trademark of Lord Chaitanya's movement.
The incarnation who establishes the process for an age; Lord Chaitanya for Kali-yuga.
The complete, congregational glorification of the Lord, including chanting and book distribution.
The 'great drum' of book distribution, whose sound is heard all over the world.
A limb or process of devotional service; the nine angas go on side by side.
A renunciant in the fourth spiritual order of life.
The mantra invoking Chaitanya and His associates, chanted before the maha-mantra.
A bona fide disciplic succession or spiritual tradition.
Krishna's supreme spiritual abode, glimpsed in the mood of Harinam.
